title: The Boston Tea Party Was Not a Tax Revolt but a Chain Reaction After a London Financial Blowup
dek: The Boston Tea Party was not a tax revolt sparked by heavy taxation in North America, but a self-rescue in which a London financial crisis was passed on to North America through the lever of the East India Company—one blowup at the imperial center that finally lit the fuse of colonial revolution.
why: An intellectual history episode that cuts in through a financial crisis story, it both explains another layer of causation behind the Boston Tea Party and, through Burke's choices on the three fronts of North America, India and France, forces you to weigh anew the old binary of radical versus gradual.
who: Suited to managers choosing between radical reform and gradual improvement, and to Chinese intellectual readers who treat Anglo-American conservatism as a ready-made answer but have never read the original texts.

points.h: The Boston Tea Party was not a tax revolt
points.body: The chain behind the Boston Tea Party lies not in North American tea taxes but in the London financial storm around 1772. Some bankers shorted the East India Company too early, blew up their own positions and fled, dragging down a large number of small London financial institutions with them; the East India Company's funding chain also tightened, with roughly two-thirds of its tea sitting in warehouses. The solution Britain devised was to divert the tea to North America for clearance sales, which looked perfectly steady on the surface: it would both free the East India Company and preserve a symbolic tea tax. But what North Americans saw was not the price of tea, but Londoners once again using the colonies to fill the hole of their own financial crisis. One self-rescue at the imperial center thus became the fuse of North American independence. Burke lived in just such an empire where everything was tangled together: trouble in far-off India had to be sent to North America on the other side of the globe to be unwound.

points.h: Burke was not a thinker but a House of Commons politician
points.body: Burke was later placed in the history of political thought, but Jiang Yuan reminds us: he was essentially not a cloistered thinker but an Irish-born British MP. As a young man he went to London to study law, then switched to politics, served as secretary to the Marquess of Rockingham, and entered Parliament through a rotten borough controlled by the party leader. The Burke we read today is overwhelmingly not academic works but parliamentary speeches and letters to his Bristol constituency. Two great things in his career: one was promoting Anglo-American reconciliation, the other was leading the impeachment of Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General of India. Precisely because he was this kind of practical politician, his writing does not push ideas to extremes and always considers real difficulties and concessions—this is both why he became a symbol of conservatism for later ages and the filter we should remove when rereading him: he was a man who made judgments, not a prophet who wrote systems.

points.h: An MP is not a loudspeaker for his constituency
points.body: The North American colonies insisted they had no representation in the British Parliament, but Londoners had their own account: the House of Commons adopted virtual representation, and an MP did not represent the gains and losses of some district or place but used independent judgment to act for the whole kingdom—including the colonies. Burke's attitude was honestly embodied in the Bristol episode: as the MP elected by the Bristol constituency, he voted in favor of a free trade bill that damaged Bristol's port monopoly interests, and wrote that what was good for Britain would ultimately be good for Bristol too. In his view, representation was not carrying the constituency's voice into Parliament but representing the whole nation through one's own independent judgment as a gentleman. The people of Bristol understood this logic and promptly replaced him at the next election; he then returned to a rotten borough with almost no voters and continued as an MP. Whether this logic counts as democracy is another question, but it at least challenges an intuition—representative government need not be realized only through one-person-one-vote territorial representation.

points.h: The East India Company's double standard was the real institutional evil
points.body: Burke's impeachment of Hastings was ostensibly aimed at one man but actually at an institutional double standard. The East India Company was both a company and half a government ruling India: when you asked it to bear governing responsibility for famine and for deaths by the tens of thousands, it said it was only a company and making money for shareholder dividends was enough; but turn around and it had an army, could fight and sign treaties with Indian princes, and take over taxation and justice. Neither a pure company nor a pure government, this state created a huge arbitrage space—war was individual glory, profits went to itself, and the cost of governing failure was left to Indians and the empire to backstop. Adam Smith criticized the East India Company for the same reason. Burke later abandoned mere institutional cleanup and took the dramatic impeachment route, aiming to turn the India question into a moral spectacle. Hastings was finally found entirely blameless by the House of Lords, but British rule over India turned a corner from then on, from a governance that had blended into Indian society to a clearer racially segregated rule.

Burke is often simplified into an antique who opposed all reform, but the real thrust of conservatism is not whether to reform but how. Any reform must first examine real difficulties and actual benefits, rather than kicking down the existing institutional edifice with a theoretically perfect blueprint and building a new one out of thin air. Burke saw society as an organism that grew naturally, not a machine that could be reassembled according to a blueprint, so he preferred patching existing goods to risking abstract ideals. This judgment fits British experience: Britain was never a country that built tall buildings on flat ground; traditions like Magna Carta and the common law were themselves rounds of old bottles filled with new wine through reform. But Jiang Yuan also points out its blind spot: Burke's ideal picture always contained an imagination of a tamed, contented lower class, and when ordinary people began to demand the rights of human beings as such, this gradualist language could no longer answer.

points.h: From the liberties of Englishmen to the liberties of man
points.body: The protest logic of the North American colonies in the 1760s was originally entirely English: we are Englishmen, and what we want are rights under the common law and no taxation without representation. But by 1775 and 1776, this set of English liberties was no longer enough to protect them, and colonial argument escalated from the liberties of Englishmen to the liberties of man as such. The Declaration of Independence no longer said we are British subjects but instead said all men are created equal and born free. Burke's lifelong strategy of reconciliation with America was always to keep North America within the framework of English liberties; he did not believe people could start from scratch out of thin air. North America's decade-long crossing from the language of British constitutionalism to the language of natural rights is precisely a lesson for gradualism: gradual reform depends on a window of time, and when the speed and scope of institutional adjustment cannot keep up with external pressure, the same demand turns from a path of improvement into a reason for revolution.

points.h: Gentlemanly mutual trust was the chassis of the Industrial Revolution
points.body: The Industrial Revolution is usually told as the story of Watt and the spinning jenny, but Jiang Yuan adds a condition rarely mentioned: the credit infrastructure among strangers. Once the commercial radius expands, you must trust a bill of exchange issued by a London merchant you have never met, trust that a canal fund launched by someone you have never heard of will not cheat you. Such mutual trust cannot be maintained by blood ties and local roots; it can only rely on a universal norm—be a decent man, be a gentleman. The emerging industrial and commercial classes actively imitated and shared this gentlemanly ethic, and credit had its endorsement: a Manchester factory owner could sell goods to a distant merchant, and what the other side trusted was not necessarily the goods themselves but that the identity of a gentleman within the system would not be adulterated. This moral consensus amounted to a social operating system outside the formal legal system. Its hint for today is: reforming property rules is easy, cultivating a moral consensus in which strangers can entrust things to one another is far harder.

points.h: The Chinese-speaking world borrowed Burke to bid farewell to revolution
points.body: Burke's fame in Chinese intellectual circles was largely propped up by the farewell-to-revolution current of thought after the 1990s. Jiang Yuan exposes this borrowed relationship: the narrative that improvement is superior to revolution sounds very reasonable, but it is often using Burke's name to vent one's own pent-up feelings. If you really open Burke, you will see a great deal that looks ancient and off-key today—his candid acceptance of a hierarchical society, his expectation of a tamed people, his undisguised trust in elite politics. Burke's own thought is not equal to the Burke shaped in the Chinese context. The reminder this contrast gives readers is direct: when we turn a historical figure into a banner for our own position, the question most worth asking is not whether he was right back then, but whom we are actually talking about by borrowing him.

terms.def: Because constituency boundaries had not been adjusted for centuries, many parliamentary seats corresponded to extremely small or even deserted populations and were often controlled by magnates.
The view that the House of Commons as a whole could represent all subjects, with MPs acting on independent judgment rather than corresponding district by district to constituency populations.

quotes.text: Burke was not a thinker, he was not a university professor, nor a man who made money by writing books, not a literary man of letters—he was a politician.

You will have a protected, contented, industrious and docile people; you are taught to seek and acknowledge the happiness found in every condition, and the true moral equality of mankind lies in this.

This conservatism does not support reform, does not mean absolutely refusing reform, but means that whenever each reform is raised, one must consider its real influence, some real difficulties, and make the improvement that can actually be brought about on this real basis truly take hold, rather than saying that because of some theoretical good I will overturn the existing system.
